aliasing_rules: R1 Normalization: matching is case-insensitive and treats '-', '_' and ' ' as equivalent separators (data_analysis = Data Analysis = data-analysis). Orthographic variants are never separate capabilities.
R2 One home: every observed string maps to exactly one term — its primary function judged by the deliverable it produces, not the tool it uses.

R3 Venue rule: strings naming where work happens (a chain, network, runtime or domain label — base, solana, evm, web3, onchain) are rejected; strings naming the medium of a deliverable (a programming language — python, solidity) map to the corresponding work term.

R4 Vendor rule: vendor/product names map by the function stated in the string (brave-search-tool -> research.web-research; tavily-extractor-tool -> data.collection) and are rejected when no function is stated (nillion, cdp, wow).
R5 Concatenation rule: a field containing several capabilities jammed into one string is rejected as malformed; each part is covered by its own term.
R6 Function over actor: strings naming roles, attributes, prices or commercial terms (founder, autonomous, zero-spend) are rejected; capabilities are observable functions with a deliverable.

hard_cases.argument: Two taggers could split: site QA (engineering.testing) vs security audit (security.audit). We place it in security.audit because in this corpus it co-occurs with json-validation/data-quality on auditor agents whose deliverable is a findings report about a live site's posture, and because 'audit' everywhere else in the corpus (api-security-review, onchain-audit, smart-contract-audit) is security-flavoured. The definition of engineering.testing explicitly claims documentation/API audits so the boundary is: audits of a running site's posture -> security.audit; audits of artefacts against a spec -> engineering.testing.

Both name technologies, but a language names the medium of the deliverable (code written in Python) while a chain names the venue where value sits; the same contract developer is recognisably the same capability on any EVM chain. Rule R3 makes the call mechanical: medium maps, venue rejects. Two taggers applying R3 tag all 15 such strings identically.

hard_cases.case: x402 and its variants (x402-payments, http-402, base-usdc-x402, usdc)
hard_cases.argument: x402 is a protocol, so protocol-interop (platform) tempts; but every observed use is an agent offering to take or make machine payments — the deliverable is settled value, not interop. Commerce.x402-payments wins under R2 (judge by deliverable). 'usdc'/'base-usdc' name the asset those payments settle in within this ecosystem, so they follow x402 rather than being rejected as venue labels; the asset is part of the payment function's definition here, unlike bare 'base' which names no function.

governance_proposal: One page, sized for a two-person team. (1) The term list is a versioned JSON file in a public repo; the registry renders it. (2) Anyone proposes a term by pull request containing: the term id, a definition that passes the substitution test (two readers tag the same task identically), and links to at least two live agents or tasks already using the string in the wild — no speculative terms. (3) Aliases are data, not debate: a PR that only adds a maps_from alias for an observed string merges on one maintainer's review within 7 days (lazy consensus; silence is consent). New terms and rejections need both maintainers. (4) Terms are never deleted, only deprecated with a pointer to their successor, so old profiles keep resolving. (5) Quarterly, a maintainer re-runs the corpus collector against the named registries and opens one bulk PR mapping or rejecting every new string; the coverage checker (0 uncovered) is CI for the repo. Total steady-state cost: roughly one hour a month.
